title: Verity AI — hosting & throughput probe
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and burst concurrency for a real-time summarization product. Customer leaning towards Redwood Dedicated for predictable tail latency but wants a hosted pilot and a private VPC option discussion. Agreed to run a 2-week token/sec benchmark with synthetic streaming traces and to share SOC2 + KMS notes.
next_steps: Alex to share Dedicated pricing sheet and baseline hosted rates
Priya to propose benchmark plan (trace template + ingest script)
James to provide sample traffic histogram and SLAs target by 2026-12-10
action_items: Alex Chen: send Dedicated vs Hosted pricing with burst options by 2026-12-08
Priya Nambiar: upload benchmark harness + instructions to shared drive by 2026-12-09
James Park: export 7-day token/sec histogram and p95 logs by 2026-12-10
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-06 15:30 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), James Park (Verity CTO), Lina Morales (Lead Eng), Omar Rizvi (Infra)

Summary (auto): initial sizing & hosting discussion, follow-ups around benchmarks and security docs.

[00:00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:00:05] James Park: yeah good, loud and clear, thanks Alex.
[00:00:11] Alex Chen: cool, quick agenda — we want to understand your p95 targets, typical concurrency, and requirements for hosting model: hosted, dedicated, or private vpc. Also call out any security gating. Priya will jump into performance options.
[00:00:26] Priya Nambiar: hi all, quick intro from me — I'm the SE on latency/throughput. I'll ask a few clarifying q's and then sketch what a bench would look like.
[00:00:34] Lina Morales: hi, thanks, Lina here. We build a real-time meeting summarization pipeline, so small-ish prompts but streaming responses. Latency matters for user experience.
[00:00:43] Omar Rizvi: and we have some compliance folks so VPC + KMS will probably be required if things go prod.
[00:00:50] Priya Nambiar: ok makes sense. Can you share ballpark p95 for response time you want at prod?
[00:00:56] James Park: internally we use a 500ms p95 goal for token streaming start, ideally closer to 300ms, but realistically we may accept 800ms if throughput is high.
[00:01:07] Alex Chen: helpful — so 300–500ms target, with some wiggle to 800ms for heavy loads. What's your concurrency at peak?
[00:01:15] Lina Morales: peaks at about 450 concurrent user streams. Each stream averages 60 tokens/sec while users are active, spikes to 120 for some flows. Overall token/sec at peak ~27k tokens/sec.
[00:01:28] Priya Nambiar: ok that's a useful number set. Is the 450 concurrent streams long lived or bursty?
[00:01:34] James Park: mostly long lived during a morning rush — sessions last 3–6 minutes, not perpetual, but we can have sustained windows of 20–25 minutes with that concurrency.
[00:01:43] Priya Nambiar: got it. Are you currently hosting models yourselves or using another provider?
[00:01:48] Lina Morales: we're on MultiNode Labs for inference today; been seeing p95 jitter and fallback spikes — sometimes cold starts take too long. We're evaluating Redwood for better tail guarantees and cost predictability.
[00:01:59] Alex Chen: thanks. For streaming workloads the key levers are instance sizing, continuous batching thresholds, kv-cache warmup, and prefix caching. Our Dedicated pools give much more predictable tail latency because you control GPU pools and don't get noisy neighbor interference.
[00:02:14] James Park: can you quantify — like how many tokens/sec per GPU for models like Llama2-13B or Mistral-like?
[00:02:22] Priya Nambiar: rough ballpark — depends on quantization and sequence length. For Llama2-13B with q4 variants we typically see 1.2k–2.5k tokens/sec sustained per A100-class GPU for streaming decode with 8–16 token generation windows, and p95 per-token latency in the 30–70ms range; end-to-end first-token p95 can be 200–400ms depending on routing and cache warmup. For larger models or fp16 the numbers drop.
[00:02:48] Omar Rizvi: that 1.2k–2.5k per GPU means we need roughly 11–23 GPUs for 27k token/sec?
[00:02:55] Priya Nambiar: yes ballpark. But with batching, multiplexing and prefix caching you can often reduce effective requirement, e.g., with a good prefix KV warmup for repeated client prompts we sometimes cut tokens/sec demand by 20–30%.
[00:03:07] James Park: interesting. What's the tradeoff with latency though when you batch more aggressively?
[00:03:12] Priya Nambiar: batching increases per-token throughput but can add a fixed batch-formation latency; Redwood has dynamic batching with latency SLOs — you can set a max wait threshold like 10–30ms, and the system will prioritize low-latency paths for streams flagged as latency-sensitive. That way you get throughput gains without regularly violating your p95.
[00:03:28] Lina Morales: hmm, we can't tolerate batching waits over 40ms for first tokens.
[00:03:33] Priya Nambiar: understood — we default to aggressive low-wait routing for live streaming. For background or bulk generation you can use high-throughput routes.
[00:03:42] Alex Chen: question — are you planning to encrypt keys with a managed KMS or customer-managed?
[00:03:47] Omar Rizvi: customer-managed KMS is preferred. Our security team will want HSM-backed keys if possible.
[00:03:53] Priya Nambiar: we support KMS integration in Private and Dedicated; hosted can integrate with customer KMS in the VPC private deployment. We also produce audit logs and detailed token-level traces in the console.
[00:04:04] James Park: ok good. About cold starts — what's the warmup pattern for KV cache? If a user opens a new meeting, how long until the cache warms and p95 improves?
[00:04:13] Priya Nambiar: cache behavior depends on prefix reuse. If you have repeated system prompts or similar histories, warmup is essentially immediate for later tokens; otherwise you see a 1–3 request warmup where early requests are slower. We can pre-warm keys if you hand us a set of representative prefixes during pilot.
[00:04:28] Lina Morales: we'll provide a set. Also, we want to see real p95 numbers, not just theoretical. Can we run a benchmark with our traffic pattern?
[00:04:36] Alex Chen: yes — standard approach is a 2-week pilot: 3-day hosted baseline, then a dedicated pool sandbox run with identical trace replay. Priya will prepare a harness that replays your trace with configurable concurrency and token rates.
[00:04:50] Priya Nambiar: I'll include scripts to emulate jitter, long sessions, and token bursts. We'll also export per-route p95, tail histograms, and token/sec plating.
[00:04:59] James Park: what's the instrumentation cadence? We need p95, p99, CPU/GPU utilization, and queue lengths.
[00:05:06] Priya Nambiar: we'll export p50/p95/p99 by model variant and by route every 1s/10s window and include GPU metrics via exporters.
[00:05:13] Omar Rizvi: and can we validate SLOs via canary routing — like 10% to hosted then failover to dedicated?
[00:05:19] Alex Chen: yes rollout policies support canary/gradual shifts and automatic fallback between model variants or regions if latency spikes.
[00:05:26] Lina Morales: any gotchas for on-premises or VPC private?
[00:05:30] Priya Nambiar: for private on-prem we ship a control plane plus customer-owned data plane; network egress and kernel compatibility can affect cold start windows. We do a health checklist before pilot.
[00:05:40] James Park: pricing question — how do burst credits work? We have predictable baseline and rare spikes.
[00:05:46] Alex Chen: Dedicated is commit-based with burst pools: you buy baseline capacity and enable burst to pay-as-you-go above that. We can model your 95th-percentile monthly to suggest a commit level and show cost tradeoffs.
[00:05:57] James Park: sounds good. If we start with hosted, how long before we can migrate to Dedicated or Private?
[00:06:03] Priya Nambiar: migration can be done with minimal code change — same API and model pins. Moving route policy and capacity takes days for simple setups; for private on-prem it's usually 4–8 weeks for full provisioning.
[00:06:13] Alex Chen: any security blockers from you?
[00:06:16] Omar Rizvi: SOC2 type 2 report and encryption in transit at minimum. Also RBAC and audit logs.
[00:06:21] Priya Nambiar: we can share SOC2 docs; RBAC/SSO supported with SAML/OIDC.
[00:06:26] James Park: ok next I'm going to share our 7-day traffic histogram and a couple of p95 outliers. We'll aim to get those to you by Friday.
[00:06:33] Alex Chen: perfect. Priya, can you outline the benchmark plan briefly now?
[00:06:37] Priya Nambiar: plan: 1) collect trace (James) 2) run hosted baseline for 72 hours with trace replay, collect p95/p99 and per-token latencies 3) run Dedicated sandbox (same trace) with a pool sized to predicted commit, 4) run stress bursts to validate fallback and failover, 5) analyze and recommend commit + batching config. We'll deliver a report and a suggested config.
[00:07:00] Lina Morales: what about metrics for streaming quality? We need end-to-end time-to-first-token and per-token jitter.
[00:07:06] Priya Nambiar: included — time-to-first-token per stream, inter-token jitter, and error rates.
[00:07:12] Alex Chen: ok let's recap -- action items: Alex send pricing; Priya send bench harness; James send trace; schedule follow-ups. Any other questions?
[00:07:22] James Park: one more — do you offer quantized model variants for lower cost without big quality loss?
[00:07:27] Priya Nambiar: yes we have quant profiles and we run evals on your prompts to measure quality delta. We can surface ROUGE/BLEU style metrics or bespoke human evals.
[00:07:35] Omar Rizvi: great. End of our side.
[00:07:38] Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email with docs and the benchmark plan.
[00:07:42] [recording ends]

Notes: transcript has occasional speaker attribution glitches and minor transcription errors (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache). References: benchmark harness link (drive/verity/bench-harness), SOC2 packet (link), Dedicated pricing (sheet link).
